Discovering New EuroLeague Player Roles Using Unsupervised Learning¶

Doron and Yuval

Research question¶

Can unsupervised learning discover meaningful EuroLeague player roles directly from playing behavior, and do these roles offer useful distinctions beyond the traditional basketball positions?

Motivation¶

Modern basketball players often do not fit cleanly into the traditional positions. A lot of "forwards" shoot threes like guards, and some "guards" rebound like forwards. We want to see whether an unsupervised model, given enough statistics about how a player actually plays, groups players in a way that says more about their real role than their listed position does.

To keep this honest, we do not give the model any position label. Positions serve only as an external reference after clustering. Our main comparison is with the five traditional basketball positions (point guard, shooting guard, small forward, power forward, center), which we compiled from 365scores and Wikipedia because the EuroLeague biography data records only three broad categories (Guard, Forward, Center); the three-category label remains as a coarser, supplementary comparison. A set of discovered roles is valuable not because it contains more groups than there are positions, but if its groups have a clear basketball meaning and show distinctions that the position labels do not.

Data sources¶

We are working with three raw tables and one file we produced earlier by combining two of them:

  • euroleague_players.csv — one row per player, season, and team, with season totals (points, rebounds, assists, shooting splits, etc.).
  • euroleague_points.csv — one row per recorded shot or free-throw event, including the court coordinates of the attempt.
  • players_bio.csv — one row per player, scraped from the EuroLeague website (height, position, nationality, etc.).
  • merged_euroleague_players.csv — the shot-event table enriched with the biography columns, produced from the two files above. We treat it as something we can regenerate, not as a separate source of information.

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

RANDOM_STATE = 42
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 60)
pd.set_option("display.width", 160)
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")


def find_repo_root(start: Path, markers=("data", "notebooks")) -> Path:
    current = start.resolve()
    for candidate in [current, *current.parents]:
        if all((candidate / marker).exists() for marker in markers):
            return candidate
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"Could not find the project root from {start}")


REPO_ROOT = find_repo_root(Path(globals().get("__file__", Path.cwd())))

FIG_DIR = REPO_ROOT / "outputs" / "figures"
FIG_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

players_df = pd.read_csv(DATA_RAW / "euroleague_players.csv", low_memory=False)

bio_df = pd.read_csv(DATA_RAW / "players_bio.csv", low_memory=False)

print(f"euroleague_points.csv:  {points_df.shape[0]:,} rows, {points_df.shape[1]} columns")

Understanding the data¶

Before doing anything else, we needed to know what a row actually represents in each table, and which columns we could use to join them together.

euroleague_players.csv has one row per player, per season, per team — a player who changes teams mid-season gets a separate row for each team. euroleague_points.csv has one row per recorded shot or free-throw attempt during a game, with coord_x/coord_y marking where on the court it happened. players_bio.csv has one row per player, scraped from the EuroLeague website, and is where height and traditional position come from.

player_id is the natural key to connect euroleague_players.csv/euroleague_points.csv to players_bio.csv, since a player keeps the same player_id across seasons and teams. For connecting the two event-and-season tables to each other, we need the combination season_code + player_id + team_id, because using player_id alone would merge a player's different seasons and teams into one group.

Before combining the datasets, we checked the identifiers, coverage, and missing values that could affect the analysis.

303 rows have zero or negative minutes and 302 have zero or negative games played — mostly players who were on a roster but never actually played, so we will need to exclude or handle these separately once we start building per-minute features.

More importantly, the minutes_per_game column that comes with the file does not match minutes / games_played in 462 rows. Since we don't know how that column was computed, we decided to always derive per-game or per-minute statistics ourselves from the raw totals (minutes, points, etc.) instead of trusting the provided per-game columns.

27 players have no recorded height and 54 have no recorded position, mostly players whose EuroLeague profile page could not be scraped. This first check counts only NaN values, so 27 is the number of players with no height value at all, not necessarily every player without a usable height. Most recorded heights fall roughly between 180 and 210 cm, so height looks like a plausible feature for later; we keep it as a candidate and decide later how to handle the players without a usable height. position is never going to be a model input anyway — we only need it later for comparison, so its missing values matter less.

The set of event types recorded in euroleague_points.csv is not the same across all seasons: E2007 only has 7 action codes, E2008-E2014 has 10 (including separate codes for dunks, layups, and blocked shots), E2015-E2016 drops back to 7, and from E2017 onward there are only 5 (just made/missed two- and three-point attempts plus free throws). This means we can't build a "dunk rate" or "blocked-shot rate" feature that covers the whole 2007-2025 range — at best it would only be usable for the E2008-E2014 seasons, so we are leaving those out of the feature set for now.

Combining the data¶

With the three tables understood, the next question was how to join them without losing or duplicating rows.

In [12]:
players_with_bio = players_df.merge(bio_df, on="player_id", how="left", validate="m:1")

print(f"euroleague_players.csv: {len(players_df)} rows in, {len(players_with_bio)} rows out")
print("player_id values with no biography match:",
      (~players_df["player_id"].isin(bio_df["player_id"])).sum(), "(from euroleague_players.csv),",
      (~points_df["player_id"].isin(bio_df["player_id"])).sum(), "(from euroleague_points.csv)")

euroleague_players.csv: 6307 rows in, 6307 rows out
player_id values with no biography match: 0 (from euroleague_players.csv), 0 (from euroleague_points.csv)

Joining euroleague_players.csv to players_bio.csv on player_id with validate="m:1" kept all 6,307 rows, and every player_id in both the season table and the event table has a biography row. Since player_id is unique in players_bio.csv, a plain left join adds height and position without duplicating or losing rows. The same join applied to the event table is how merged_euroleague_players.csv (the file we produced earlier) was built: euroleague_points.csv left-joined with players_bio.csv on player_id. This notebook does not need that large event-level table, so we do not build it here; it can always be regenerated from the two raw files.

In [13]:
season_team_stats = players_df[["season_code", "player_id", "team_id"]].drop_duplicates()
season_team_events = points_df[["season_code", "player_id", "team_id"]].drop_duplicates()

only_in_stats = season_team_stats.merge(season_team_events, on=["season_code", "player_id", "team_id"],
                                         how="left", indicator=True)
only_in_stats = only_in_stats[only_in_stats["_merge"] == "left_only"]
print(f"player-season-team rows in euroleague_players.csv with no matching shot events: "
      f"{len(only_in_stats)} of {len(season_team_stats)}")

player-season-team rows in euroleague_players.csv with no matching shot events: 459 of 6307

459 player-season-team rows in euroleague_players.csv have no matching rows at all in euroleague_points.csv. At this point that looked like a possible gap in the event data -- those rows would have no shot-location features -- so we kept them in the season-level table, which still has their totals (points, rebounds, etc.), and returned to them once we could compare the event data with the season totals.

58 player-seasons are split across two teams (a mid-season transfer), each with its own row. We are keeping these as separate rows rather than merging them, since the whole point of using season_code + player_id + team_id as the key is to let a player's role differ by team.

One more thing worth noting: players_bio.csv also has club_code/club_name, which is the player's club at the time the page was scraped — not their team in a given season. We use team_id from euroleague_players.csv/euroleague_points.csv for anything historical, and only use the biography table for things that don't change with time, like height.

Understanding shot coordinates¶

euroleague_points.csv gives us coord_x/coord_y for every recorded attempt, which is potentially a rich source of playing-style information — where on the court a player likes to shoot from. Before we can turn that into features, we need to know what the numbers mean. We could not find a documented definition of the coordinate system in the dataset source, so we interpreted it using the spatial distribution of the shots.

The first thing we noticed is that free throws (action_id == "FTM") all carry the exact same coordinate, (-1, -1), for all 140,926 free-throw rows. That makes sense — a free throw is always taken from the same spot, so there's nothing to record — but it also means this value is a placeholder, not a real location, so we excluded free throws from anything spatial and kept only genuine field-goal attempts (makes and misses, two- and three-point).

In [15]:
SHOT_ACTION_IDS = ["2FGA", "2FGAB", "2FGM", "3FGA", "3FGAB", "3FGM", "DUNK", "LAYUPATT", "LAYUPMD"]
TWO_PT_IDS = ["2FGA", "2FGAB", "2FGM", "DUNK", "LAYUPATT", "LAYUPMD"]
THREE_PT_IDS = ["3FGA", "3FGAB", "3FGM"]

shots = points_df[points_df["action_id"].isin(SHOT_ACTION_IDS)].copy()
print(f"Shot attempts (field-goal makes and misses): {len(shots):,} of {len(points_df):,} rows")
print(f"Missing coordinates among shot attempts: {shots[['coord_x', 'coord_y']].isna().any(axis=1).sum()}")

shots["shot_type"] = np.where(shots["action_id"].isin(THREE_PT_IDS), "Three-point", "Two-point")

Shot attempts (field-goal makes and misses): 614,219 of 755,145 rows

                                                     random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")

Both plots show a single half-court, not two mirrored halves: two-point attempts form a dense fan close to one point near the bottom of the plot, and three-point attempts form a clear arc farther out, with denser patches on the sides where the corner threes are. In this pooled view, the zone letters also form spatially coherent regions — the near-basket zone sits inside the two-point fan, and the two three-point-arc zones sit on either side. That shows the zones are spatially structured overall, but a plot pooled over all 19 seasons cannot tell us whether each letter marks the same area in every season.

The dense point at the center of the two-point fan is very close to coord_x = 0, coord_y = 0 — we checked this directly using dunk attempts, which by definition happen right at the rim, and their median location is exactly (0, 0). We also checked that this holds up across seasons and across both teams in a game, so we're treating it as a stable convention, not something we need to correct per game or per team.

Based on this, we decided to:

  • Use (0, 0) as the basket location and compute shot distance as sqrt(coord_x**2 + coord_y**2).
  • Keep that distance in raw coordinate units rather than claiming it is centimeters or any other physical unit, since we have no documentation confirming the scale.
  • Treat coord_x as the left-right position and coord_y as the distance from the basket toward half-court.
  • Not build separate dunk/layup/blocked-shot features, since those event types are only recorded consistently between E2008 and E2014 (see above).

Building the player-season-team feature table¶

After checking the identifiers and shot coordinates, we were ready to combine everything into one table with a single row per season, player, and team. We used euroleague_players.csv as the base, since it already has the granularity we need, and added biography information and shot-location statistics on top of it using the joins we already validated above.

In [18]:
features = players_with_bio.copy()
print(f"Base table: {len(features)} rows, one per season_player_id "
      f"(unique: {features['season_player_id'].is_unique})")

Base table: 6307 rows, one per season_player_id (unique: True)

As we saw earlier, 27 players have no recorded height (NaN) and 54 have no recorded position. Height is a plausible model feature, so we kept the missing values as they are rather than filling them now, since we had not defined the final eligible training sample yet. Whether height enters the model, and how to handle players without a usable height, was still an open decision at this point. Whatever we decided, we would not estimate height from traditional position, since position is reserved for comparing the discovered roles afterwards and should not influence how the clusters are formed in the first place.

Position itself is never going to be a clustering feature, so a missing position does not remove a player from the table. We are not filling it with the most common position either, since that would invent a label and distort the later comparison between our clusters and the traditional positions. Rows with a missing position stay in the feature table and are simply left out of any analysis that explicitly compares clusters against position.

We already found that the provided minutes_per_game does not match minutes / games_played for 462 rows, so we are calculating every rate feature ourselves from the raw totals instead of trusting the columns that come with the file. We used minutes as the denominator for playing-style volume and expressed every rate per 40 minutes (season total / minutes * 40). A EuroLeague regulation game lasts 40 minutes, so a per-40 value reads as the rate on the scale of one full regulation game. This does not assume that any player actually plays 40 minutes; it only puts players with very different playing time on a common scale. The per-36 convention common in NBA analysis would differ only by the constant factor 40/36 for every rate, so after standardization it would give exactly the same standardized values and the same clustering; we chose per 40 because it is easier to interpret in the EuroLeague context. A row with zero minutes does not have a meaningful rate, so we left those as missing rather than zero, and kept a flag so they can be filtered out later.

In [19]:
features["has_positive_minutes"] = features["minutes"] > 0
features["has_positive_games"] = features["games_played"] > 0

REGULATION_GAME_MINUTES = 40
PER_40_SOURCE_COLUMNS = {
    "points_per_40": "points",
    "two_point_attempts_per_40": "two_points_attempted",
    "three_point_attempts_per_40": "three_points_attempted",
    "free_throw_attempts_per_40": "free_throws_attempted",
    "offensive_rebounds_per_40": "offensive_rebounds",
    "defensive_rebounds_per_40": "defensive_rebounds",
    "assists_per_40": "assists",
    "steals_per_40": "steals",
    "turnovers_per_40": "turnovers",
    "blocks_per_40": "blocks_favour",
    "fouls_committed_per_40": "fouls_committed",
    "fouls_received_per_40": "fouls_received",
}

for per_40_col, total_col in PER_40_SOURCE_COLUMNS.items():
    features[per_40_col] = np.where(
        features["has_positive_minutes"],
        features[total_col] / features["minutes"] * REGULATION_GAME_MINUTES,
        np.nan,
    )

print(f"Rows without positive minutes (per-40 values left as NaN): "
      f"{(~features['has_positive_minutes']).sum()}")
features[["player", "minutes", "points", "points_per_40", "assists", "assists_per_40"]].sample(
    3, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

We also calculated a few shot-selection ratios directly from the season totals: how many field-goal attempts a player took in total, and what share of those were twos versus threes, plus a free-throw rate relative to field-goal attempts. A share is undefined when its denominator is zero, so we left those as missing instead of filling them with a mean, median, or zero. The shooting percentages that come with the file (two_points_percentage, three_points_percentage, free_throws_percentage) stay in the table as descriptive candidates — we are not deciding yet whether efficiency measures belong in the clustering features. valuation and plus_minus also stay in the table for reference, but they combine playing quality with playing style, so we are marking them as excluded from the model rather than treating them as candidate features.

In [20]:
features["field_goal_attempts"] = features["two_points_attempted"] + features["three_points_attempted"]
has_fga = features["field_goal_attempts"] > 0

features["two_point_attempt_share"] = np.where(
    has_fga, features["two_points_attempted"] / features["field_goal_attempts"], np.nan)
features["three_point_attempt_share"] = np.where(
    has_fga, features["three_points_attempted"] / features["field_goal_attempts"], np.nan)
features["free_throw_attempt_rate"] = np.where(
    has_fga, features["free_throws_attempted"] / features["field_goal_attempts"], np.nan)

print(f"Rows with zero field-goal attempts (shares left as NaN): {(~has_fga).sum()}")
features[["player", "field_goal_attempts", "two_point_attempt_share",
          "three_point_attempt_share", "free_throw_attempt_rate"]].sample(3, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

Before aggregating the shot events into player-season-team statistics, it is worth being clear about what a missing value means in this table, because it is not the same problem in every column. Almost every missing zone value belongs to a free throw, where a regular shot zone does not apply. Free throws also use (-1, -1) as a fixed coordinate rather than a real location, so we kept them for free-throw volume (already covered by the season totals) but excluded them from anything spatial. A small number of genuine field-goal attempts, 93 of the 614,219 we identified earlier, use that same (-1, -1) placeholder and are missing a zone for the same reason — we excluded those 93 events from the coordinate and zone aggregation as well, without deleting them from the underlying event data. Their effect is negligible next to 614,219 recorded attempts.

We are also leaving out fastbreak, second_chance, and points_off_turnover from the feature table. These columns were not recorded consistently in the earlier seasons, and a missing value there means the information was never collected, not that the event was known not to be a fast break or a second-chance shot. Filling them with zero or with the most common value would invent history we don't actually have, so we are not including them in the main table for the full 19-season range. They could still be worth a separate analysis restricted to the seasons that do record them.

In [21]:
shots["shot_category"] = np.where(shots["action_id"].isin(THREE_PT_IDS), "three_point", "two_point")
shots["is_made"] = shots["action_id"].isin(["2FGM", "3FGM", "DUNK", "LAYUPMD"])

has_sentinel_coord = (shots["coord_x"] == -1) & (shots["coord_y"] == -1)
valid_shots = shots[~has_sentinel_coord].copy()
valid_shots["raw_shot_distance"] = np.sqrt(valid_shots["coord_x"] ** 2 + valid_shots["coord_y"] ** 2)

print(f"Field-goal attempts: {len(shots):,}")
print(f"Field-goal attempts with the free-throw sentinel coordinate: {has_sentinel_coord.sum()}")
print(f"Field-goal attempts usable for spatial aggregation: {len(valid_shots):,}")

We then aggregated the event data by season_code, player_id, and team_id — the same key we use everywhere else — into coverage counts, shot-type shares, coordinate summaries, and zone shares.

In [22]:
KEY = ["season_code", "player_id", "team_id"]

coverage = shots.groupby(KEY).agg(
    shot_event_count=("game_point_id", "size"),
    two_point_event_count=("shot_category", lambda s: (s == "two_point").sum()),
    three_point_event_count=("shot_category", lambda s: (s == "three_point").sum()),
).reset_index()

has_events = coverage["shot_event_count"] > 0
coverage["event_two_point_attempt_share"] = np.where(
    has_events, coverage["two_point_event_count"] / coverage["shot_event_count"], np.nan)
coverage["event_three_point_attempt_share"] = np.where(
    has_events, coverage["three_point_event_count"] / coverage["shot_event_count"], np.nan)

print(f"Player-season-team groups with at least one field-goal attempt: {len(coverage)}")

Player-season-team groups with at least one field-goal attempt: 5834
In [23]:
spatial = valid_shots.groupby(KEY).agg(
    valid_spatial_shot_count=("game_point_id", "size"),
    mean_lateral_shot_position=("coord_x", "mean"),
    lateral_shot_position_std=("coord_x", "std"),
    mean_longitudinal_shot_position=("coord_y", "mean"),
    longitudinal_shot_position_std=("coord_y", "std"),
    mean_raw_shot_distance=("raw_shot_distance", "mean"),
    median_raw_shot_distance=("raw_shot_distance", "median"),
    raw_shot_distance_std=("raw_shot_distance", "std"),
).reset_index()

single_shot_groups = (spatial["valid_spatial_shot_count"] == 1).sum()
print(f"Player-season-team groups with only one valid shot: {single_shot_groups} "
      f"(their standard-deviation columns are left as NaN -- a spread cannot be computed "
      f"from a single point, so this is not the same thing as zero spread)")

Player-season-team groups with only one valid shot: 126 (their standard-deviation columns are left as NaN -- a spread cannot be computed from a single point, so this is not the same thing as zero spread)

The exact boundaries of the EuroLeague zone letters are not documented anywhere we could find, so rather than inventing our own coordinate cutoffs for "paint" or "corner three", we used the recorded zone values as they are and calculated an attempt share for each one as a candidate feature. Any naming of what a zone likely represents is our own reading of the scatter plot above, not an official definition. At this point we had not checked whether each letter keeps the same meaning across seasons; whether the zone shares are suitable model inputs is decided later, when we select the final features.

In [24]:
zone_counts = valid_shots.groupby(KEY)["zone"].value_counts().unstack(fill_value=0)
zone_counts.columns = [f"zone_{c.lower()}_attempt_share" for c in zone_counts.columns]
zone_totals = zone_counts.sum(axis=1)
zone_shares = zone_counts.div(zone_totals, axis=0).reset_index()
zone_shares["valid_zone_shot_count"] = zone_totals.values

event_features = coverage.merge(spatial, on=KEY, how="left").merge(zone_shares, on=KEY, how="left")
print(f"Event-derived feature rows: {len(event_features)}")

Event-derived feature rows: 5834

Before joining the event features onto the season-level table, we compared the two sources of shot-attempt counts, since they were collected independently: euroleague_players.csv already has season totals for two- and three-point attempts, and we just built our own counts from the event data. If the two disagreed by a lot, it would mean our shot-location profile only covers part of a player's actual attempts.

In [25]:
season_totals = players_df[KEY + ["two_points_attempted", "three_points_attempted"]].copy()

                                  on=KEY, how="left")

    ["two_point_event_count", "three_point_event_count"]].fillna(0)

                                             comparison["three_points_attempted"])
comparison["field_goal_attempts_event"] = (comparison["two_point_event_count"] +
                                            comparison["three_point_event_count"])

The two sources agree almost perfectly: only a single player-season-team row out of 6,307 shows a difference, one player in E2017 whose event count is 15 shots higher than the season total. That is not something we can resolve from the data we have, so we are leaving it as a documented mismatch rather than adjusting either number. Given how rare this is, we used the season totals as the source for volume features (points, attempts, rebounds, and the per-40 rates above) and the event data only for coordinate- and zone-based features, which is what the event data is actually needed for.

We left-joined the event features onto the base table on season_code, player_id, and team_id, and then went back to the 459 rows without shot events to check their season totals.

The join kept all 6,307 rows. The check resolves the earlier concern about the 459 rows without shot events: according to the season totals, none of them attempted a field goal, and none played more than 29.2 minutes, across at most 5 games. These players had no shot location to record, so the rows are not missing spatial observations for real field-goal attempts. A further 14 rows have free-throw events but never attempted a field goal, so they get event coverage but no spatial statistics. We kept all of these rows in the table and flagged them rather than dropping them or filling their shot-location features with an average, since an average location would invent a playing style for players who never took a shot.

With everything joined, we organized the columns into groups -- identifiers, descriptive and comparison fields, participation and coverage, season totals and rates, shooting mix, and coordinate/zone features -- which gives the complete feature table.

Every row (6,307 of 6,307) has season totals, but per-40 rates need positive minutes: 6,004 rows have them, and the remaining 303 rows correctly keep a missing per-40 value instead of a meaningless rate. Event coverage drops slightly to 5,848 rows, and valid spatial coverage to 5,834, which matches the free-throw-only rows we found above. height_cm is non-missing for 6,253 of the 6,307 rows; the rows of the 27 players without a recorded height carry through as missing, as intended (like the earlier check, this count only looks for NaN).

We also built a short data dictionary describing every column in the feature table, its source, and what a missing value means for that specific column, with a preliminary note on whether it looks like a clustering candidate, a comparison-only field, or something we are excluding; we replaced these notes with the final decisions once we selected the features.

In [31]:
def dict_row(column, group, source, definition, calculation, missing_meaning, intended_use,
             eligible, reason):
    return {"column": column, "group": group, "source": source, "definition": definition,
            "calculation": calculation, "missing_value_meaning": missing_meaning,
            "intended_use": intended_use, "eligible_for_clustering": eligible, "reason": reason}


dictionary_rows = []

for col in IDENTIFIER_COLS:
    dictionary_rows.append(dict_row(
        col, "identifier", "euroleague_players.csv", f"{col} identifier.", "as provided",
        "not applicable (identifier)", "join / lookup key", "exclude", "Identifier, not a statistic."))

             "as provided", "player's profile page could not be fully scraped",
             "post-hoc comparison only", "comparison_only",
             "Never used as a clustering input; only for comparing clusters to positions afterwards."),
    dict_row("nationality", "descriptive", "players_bio.csv", "Player nationality.",

The complete table has one row per player, season, and team, with season totals and per-40 rates, shot-selection shares, and shot-location statistics sitting alongside the identifiers and biography fields. Height, position, and every spatial feature keep their missing values exactly where the underlying data is missing, since we still need to define which player-season-team rows are eligible for training before deciding how -- or whether -- to fill anything in.

Defining the eligible modeling sample¶

With the complete feature table built, the next question is which of the 6,307 player-season-team rows have enough playing time to represent a real playing style, rather than a handful of garbage-time minutes. We started by looking at how minutes, games_played, and field_goal_attempts are distributed, with particular attention to the lower end of each distribution, since that is where the unreliable observations are concentrated.

All three variables are heavily right-skewed, and a large share of rows sit very close to zero. 10% of rows have under 8 minutes, under 2 games played, and under 2 field-goal attempts; a quarter of rows have under 84 minutes, 8 games, and 20 attempts. The median row has 268 minutes, 16 games, and 74 attempts -- a full rotation player's season -- so the low end is doing a lot of the work in deciding how much of the table is usable.

The three curves rise steeply near zero and then flatten out, which is the same story as the percentile table in chart form: there is no natural gap or elbow that separates "real" playing time from noise, just a continuous rise. That means any participation cutoff is a judgment call, not something the data picks for us on its own -- which is exactly why we compare several candidate rules below instead of picking one number outright.

We compared four candidate participation rules, each requiring a minimum number of games played and a minimum number of minutes: 5 games/100 minutes, 10 games/200 minutes, 10 games/300 minutes, and 15 games/400 minutes. For each rule we looked at how many rows it keeps, whether every season is still represented, and how many of the retained rows would still be missing shot-location data or have zero field-goal attempts -- since those would be retained by minutes/games alone but still be unusable for the spatial features.

In [34]:
PARTICIPATION_RULES = [
    ("5 games / 100 minutes", 5, 100),
    ("10 games / 200 minutes", 10, 200),
    ("10 games / 300 minutes", 10, 300),
    ("15 games / 400 minutes", 15, 400),
]

rule_comparison_rows = []
for label, min_games, min_minutes in PARTICIPATION_RULES:
    meets_rule = (features["games_played"] >= min_games) & (features["minutes"] >= min_minutes)
    retained = features[meets_rule]
    per_season_counts = retained.groupby("season_code").size()
    rule_comparison_rows.append({
        "rule": label,
        "retained_rows": int(meets_rule.sum()),
        "retained_pct": round(100 * meets_rule.mean(), 1),
        "removed_rows": int((~meets_rule).sum()),
        "seasons_represented": int(per_season_counts.shape[0]),
        "min_rows_per_season": int(per_season_counts.min()),
        "max_rows_per_season": int(per_season_counts.max()),
        "retained_missing_spatial_data": int((~retained["has_valid_spatial_data"]).sum()),
        "retained_zero_field_goal_attempts": int((retained["field_goal_attempts"] == 0).sum()),
    })

participation_rule_comparison = pd.DataFrame(rule_comparison_rows)
participation_rule_comparison

All four rules keep every one of the 19 seasons represented, so none of them concentrates the sample in particular years. Retained rows go from 4,568 (72.4%) under the loosest rule down to 2,193 (34.8%) under the strictest one. None of the four rules leaves any retained row without valid spatial data or with zero field-goal attempts -- once a player clears even the loosest games/minutes bar, they have always taken at least a handful of shots, so field_goal_attempts is not adding an eligibility constraint of its own here; it is telling us the minutes/games cutoffs already imply a minimum shot volume, not that we need a separate shot-volume rule.

Knowing how many rows each rule removes is not enough on its own -- we also wanted to know what kind of player-season-team observation gets cut, since a rule can remove only negligible-participation rows or it can start cutting into rows that still represent a real, if smaller, role.

Under the loosest rule (5 games/100 minutes), the rows it removes top out at 136.6 minutes, 21 games, 47 field-goal attempts, and 56 points across the whole season -- genuinely marginal appearances. Under the strictest rule (15 games/400 minutes), the removed rows can reach 474.7 minutes, 36 games, 232 field-goal attempts, and 305 points, which is a full partial season for a real rotation player, not a token appearance. So the stricter rules do not only remove noise: they also start cutting player-season-team observations that look like legitimate, if smaller, playing roles.

Selecting the eligible modeling sample¶

Neither keeping the most rows nor filtering hardest is automatically better. Very low-participation rows produce per-40 rates and shot-location statistics built on a handful of events, which are not a stable estimate of how someone plays. A stricter threshold guarantees more evidence behind every rate, but it pushes the sample toward established, high-minute rotation players and disproportionately removes short team stints, reserve roles, injuries, and mid-season transfers -- the situations the player-season-team unit of observation is meant to capture.

The three stricter alternatives all pay that second cost. 10 games / 200 minutes retains 3,679 rows against 4,568, removing 889 more player-season-team rows. 10 games / 300 minutes removes more than half of the complete table (3,410 of 6,307 rows) and brings at least one season down to only 96 eligible observations. 15 games / 400 minutes keeps only 2,193 rows (34.8%) and brings the smallest season down to 49. The comparison above also showed that the removed rows reach up to 474.7 minutes, 36 games, 232 attempts, and 305 points under the strictest rule -- separate maximums rather than necessarily one row, but clear evidence that meaningful playing time is being cut.

We selected 5 games / 100 minutes. It removes 1,739 clearly low-participation rows while keeping 4,568, 72.4% of the complete table, and it preserves all 19 seasons with between 196 and 273 eligible observations each. Every retained row already has valid spatial data and at least one field-goal attempt, so no separate shot-volume condition is needed. We are not claiming that 100 minutes makes every statistic stable, or that it is a universal basketball threshold -- it is a balance between reliability and representativeness for this dataset and our player-season-team unit of observation.

We kept 10 games / 200 minutes in reserve as a sensitivity check: once we have a clustering result, we can rerun it on that stricter sample and see whether the same role structure holds.

In [36]:

The counts match the comparison above exactly: 4,568 eligible rows, 1,739 ineligible, all 19 seasons represented with between 196 and 273 eligible rows each, and no eligible row missing spatial data or sitting at zero field-goal attempts.

We added the eligibility flag to the same complete feature table rather than creating a filtered copy -- all 6,307 rows are still there, now with one extra column marking which of them meet the selected participation rule. Anything that still needs every player-season-team observation (for example, describing the full 19-season dataset) can keep using the complete table, while the modeling steps can filter on eligible_for_modeling.

Missing values in the eligible sample¶

The earlier audit looked at missingness across the whole source data, before we knew which rows would even be eligible for modeling. Now that we have selected eligible_for_modeling, the population has changed, so the question is narrower and more concrete: of the 4,568 eligible player-season-team rows, which candidate modeling columns are still missing something, and what does that missing value actually mean for that column?

We build a view of the eligible rows from the complete table rather than filtering features itself, so the complete 6,307-row table stays available for anything that still needs it.

In [38]:

print(f"Eligible sample size: {len(eligible_df)}")
print(f"All eligible rows have positive minutes: {(eligible_df['minutes'] > 0).all()}")
print(f"All eligible rows have positive games played: {(eligible_df['games_played'] > 0).all()}")
print(f"All eligible rows have at least one field-goal attempt: "
      f"{(eligible_df['field_goal_attempts'] >= 1).all()}")
print(f"All eligible rows have valid spatial data: {eligible_df['has_valid_spatial_data'].all()}")
print(f"Eligible rows with exactly one valid spatial shot: "
      f"{(eligible_df['valid_spatial_shot_count'] == 1).sum()}")

The participation rule does what we hoped: every eligible row has positive minutes and games, at least one field-goal attempt, and valid spatial data, and none of them are sitting on a single shot where a standard deviation would be undefined. That already tells us the structural gaps we saw in the complete table -- rows with no recorded field-goal attempts at all -- cannot be the source of any missingness left in the eligible sample.

We then compared missingness before and after eligibility filtering for every column that is either a candidate playing-style feature or still has a missing value in the eligible sample -- height, position, the spatial location and spread features, the shot-selection shares, and the shooting-efficiency percentages. Columns with an identical missing-count pattern are grouped into one row so the table stays short.

Two columns still have missing values in the eligible sample: height_cm (31 of 4,568, down from 54 of 6,307, counting NaN values) and position (132 of 4,568, down from 172 of 6,307). Every spatial location, spread, and share column drops to zero missing rows once we restrict to the eligible sample -- both the group of 19 columns that were undefined whenever a player-season-team had no recorded field-goal attempts, and the 3 standard-deviation columns that were additionally undefined for the single-shot rows. The eligibility rule removes both problems at once, since a row cannot pass 5 games and 100 minutes without also recording more than one valid shot.

The shooting-percentage columns show zero missing values in the table above, but that is not the same as saying every value is a real measurement. A shooting percentage is only meaningful if the player actually attempted that shot type -- with zero attempts, "percentage" has no defined value, yet the source file records it as 0.0 rather than leaving it blank. We checked how often that happens inside the eligible sample.

In [40]:
for pct_col, attempt_col in [
    ("three_points_percentage", "three_points_attempted"),
    ("two_points_percentage", "two_points_attempted"),
    ("free_throws_percentage", "free_throws_attempted"),
]:
    zero_attempts = (eligible_df[attempt_col] == 0)
    n = int(zero_attempts.sum())
    print(f"{pct_col}: {n} eligible rows ({100 * n / len(eligible_df):.1f}%) have "
          f"{attempt_col} == 0, so the recorded value of 0.0 does not mean '0% shooting'")

three_points_percentage: 443 eligible rows (9.7%) have three_points_attempted == 0, so the recorded value of 0.0 does not mean '0% shooting'
two_points_percentage: 0 eligible rows (0.0%) have two_points_attempted == 0, so the recorded value of 0.0 does not mean '0% shooting'
free_throws_percentage: 34 eligible rows (0.7%) have free_throws_attempted == 0, so the recorded value of 0.0 does not mean '0% shooting'

443 eligible rows (9.7%) never attempted a three-pointer, so their three_points_percentage of 0.0 really means "no attempts," not "missed every three." free_throws_percentage has the same problem for 34 rows (0.7%), and no eligible row has zero two-point attempts, so two_points_percentage is unaffected. If shooting efficiency is used as a feature later, this needs a real decision -- treating a volume-zero player the same as a 0-for-many shooter would misrepresent both.

Putting the checks above together, the remaining missing-value questions are of four different kinds, and they do not call for the same treatment.

  • Already eliminated by the participation rule. The spatial and shot-selection columns were missing only for rows with no recorded field-goal attempt (or, for the standard-deviation columns, exactly one). No eligible row is in either situation, so nothing is left to decide.
  • Structurally undefined percentages. A 0.0 shooting percentage can mean "attempted and missed everything" or "never attempted," and only the first is a real shooting result. This needs a decision only if shooting efficiency ends up in the feature set.
  • Genuinely missing measurements. height_cm is missing for 31 eligible rows because the player's EuroLeague profile page could not be fully scraped. This has nothing to do with how the player played, so any fill must not come from playing statistics or traditional position.
  • Comparison-only missingness. position is missing for 132 eligible rows. Since position is never a clustering input, this only limits how many rows enter the later position comparison, and it must not be filled in or used to estimate any other feature.

Deciding on height and shooting efficiency as clustering features¶

Going back to the two open questions from the missing-value check: we decided to include both height and shooting efficiency in the final feature set. Height is a fixed physical attribute that plausibly shapes playing style on its own, independent of the counting and rate statistics we already have. Shooting efficiency (two-point, three-point, and free-throw percentage) captures how well a player converts the shots they take, which is a different question from how many shots they take or what kind, already covered by the volume and shot-selection features.

Including shooting efficiency means resolving the structural-zero problem above. We fixed it at the source: any percentage is set to a true missing value whenever the corresponding attempt count is zero, so "no attempts" is no longer confused with "attempted and missed everything," and we added a boolean flag recording whether the player attempted that shot type at all. two_points_percentage needs no such fix, since no eligible row has zero two-point attempts.

In [41]:
zero_three_attempts = features["three_points_attempted"] == 0
zero_ft_attempts = features["free_throws_attempted"] == 0

features["has_three_point_attempts"] = ~zero_three_attempts
features["has_free_throw_attempts"] = ~zero_ft_attempts

features.loc[zero_three_attempts, "three_points_percentage"] = np.nan
features.loc[zero_ft_attempts, "free_throws_percentage"] = np.nan

print(f"three_points_percentage set to missing: {int(zero_three_attempts.sum())} of {len(features)} rows "
      f"(full table), {int((zero_three_attempts & features['eligible_for_modeling']).sum())} of "
      f"{features['eligible_for_modeling'].sum()} eligible rows")
print(f"free_throws_percentage set to missing: {int(zero_ft_attempts.sum())} of {len(features)} rows "
      f"(full table), {int((zero_ft_attempts & features['eligible_for_modeling']).sum())} of "
      f"{features['eligible_for_modeling'].sum()} eligible rows")

three_points_percentage set to missing: 1272 of 6307 rows (full table), 443 of 4568 eligible rows
free_throws_percentage set to missing: 949 of 6307 rows (full table), 34 of 4568 eligible rows

The eligible-sample counts match the earlier diagnostic exactly -- 443 rows for three_points_percentage, 34 for free_throws_percentage -- confirming this targets the same rows we already identified, just replacing the misleading 0.0 with a real missing value. has_three_point_attempts and has_free_throw_attempts record the relevant fact -- that the player didn't take that kind of shot -- so it stays in the table once the percentage itself becomes missing. K-Means and GMM both need a complete numeric matrix, though, so we still need to decide what goes in place of the missing percentage -- we come back to that after resolving height, below.

Height is a fixed physical attribute, not something derived from playing behavior, so for the 31 eligible rows (11 unique players) still missing it, we looked up each player's height directly from an external source (Wikipedia, or 365scores.com for the one player without a Wikipedia page) rather than imputing a statistical estimate. This is a manual, cited correction, kept in data/processed/height_overrides.csv alongside the player it belongs to and the source used, rather than mixed silently into the raw biography data.

When we came back to height, a closer check of the raw biography data showed that players_bio.csv also uses 0, not only NaN, to mark a missing height -- a second sentinel that the .isna() checks above do not catch, so the earlier height counts did not include these players. We handled them the same way: each zero-height player in our modeling sample was matched to an externally verified height, preferring 365Scores when a reliable identity match was available and falling back to Wikipedia otherwise -- a verified physical measurement, not a statistical imputation. All verified heights are kept in height_overrides.csv. The override step is restricted to the player_ids listed there and replaces only NaN or 0, so it can never overwrite an existing positive height.

In [42]:
height_overrides = pd.read_csv(REPO_ROOT / "data" / "processed" / "height_overrides.csv")
print(f"Height overrides available: {height_overrides['height_cm'].notna().sum()} of {len(height_overrides)} listed players")

height_map = height_overrides.set_index("player_id")["height_cm"]
verified_height = features["player_id"].map(height_map)
recorded_nan = features["height_cm"].isna()
recorded_zero = features["height_cm"].eq(0)
height_needs_override = verified_height.notna() & (recorded_nan | recorded_zero)
features.loc[height_needs_override, "height_cm"] = verified_height[height_needs_override]

eligible_rows = features["eligible_for_modeling"]
for label, sentinel in [("NaN", recorded_nan), ("0", recorded_zero)]:
    corrected = height_needs_override & sentinel & eligible_rows
    print(f"Eligible rows corrected from a recorded height of {label}: {int(corrected.sum())} "
          f"({features.loc[corrected, 'player_id'].nunique()} players)")
print(f"Eligible rows corrected in total: {int((height_needs_override & eligible_rows).sum())}")

zero_height_players = bio_df.loc[bio_df["height_cm"].eq(0), "player_id"]
left_at_zero = recorded_zero & ~height_needs_override
print(f"Players recorded at 0 cm in players_bio.csv: {zero_height_players.nunique()}; "
      f"left unchanged: {features.loc[left_at_zero, 'player_id'].nunique()} players, "
      f"{int((left_at_zero & eligible_rows).sum())} of their rows eligible")

eligible_height = features.loc[eligible_rows, "height_cm"]
print(f"Eligible rows still missing height_cm or recorded at 0: "
      f"{int((eligible_height.isna() | eligible_height.eq(0)).sum())}")

The output keeps the two corrections apart: 31 eligible rows from 11 players had no recorded height, and 167 eligible rows from 51 players were recorded at 0 -- 198 eligible rows in total, covered by the 62 verified player IDs. Of the 58 players recorded at 0 cm in players_bio.csv, the 7 without a verified height have no eligible rows, so we left them as recorded. No eligible row is still missing a height.

Back to the shooting-percentage gap: these are players who genuinely never attempted that shot type, so there is no real percentage hiding behind the missing value -- unlike height, there is nothing to look up. Dropping the rows instead would bias the sample against exactly the low-usage and traditional-big roles this project is trying to distinguish (443 rows are 9.7% of the eligible sample). We filled the missing percentage with the median computed only from eligible rows that did attempt that shot type -- never from traditional position, for the same reason we didn't use it for height. This keeps every row in the modeling sample and gives these rows a neutral percentage rather than an invented skill level. The zero attempt volume itself stays recorded in the table (three_point_attempts_per_40, free_throw_attempts_per_40, and the two flags above); which of these columns enter the model is decided when we select the final features. The median fill only completes the feature table: when we built the modeling matrix, we replaced all three percentages with a more stable attempt-weighted estimate, which gives zero-attempt rows the sample's attempt-weighted mean instead.

In [43]:
eligible_attempted_three = features["eligible_for_modeling"] & features["has_three_point_attempts"]
eligible_attempted_ft = features["eligible_for_modeling"] & features["has_free_throw_attempts"]

three_median = features.loc[eligible_attempted_three, "three_points_percentage"].median()
ft_median = features.loc[eligible_attempted_ft, "free_throws_percentage"].median()

features["three_points_percentage"] = features["three_points_percentage"].fillna(three_median)
features["free_throws_percentage"] = features["free_throws_percentage"].fillna(ft_median)

print(f"three_points_percentage imputed with eligible-sample median: {three_median:.3f}")
print(f"free_throws_percentage imputed with eligible-sample median: {ft_median:.3f}")

print(f"Eligible rows still missing free_throws_percentage: {eligible_df['free_throws_percentage'].isna().sum()}")

That closes the shooting-percentage gap completely. Together with the height fix above, height and shooting efficiency -- the two genuine measurement gaps identified above -- are now fully resolved in the eligible sample. The only missingness left is position (132 rows), which stays exactly as it is, since it is comparison-only.

Enriching position from two external sources¶

position is comparison-only, never a clustering input, but on its own it only separates players into three broad groups (Guard, Forward, Center) and is still missing for 132 of the 4,568 eligible rows. To get a finer, more informative label for comparing against the discovered roles later, we independently looked up each unique player (player_id, matched against players_bio.csv) on Wikipedia and on 365scores.com, and normalized whatever position each site listed to one of five standard positions: Point Guard, Shooting Guard, Small Forward, Power Forward, Center. Both lookups are per player, not per player-season-team, since a player's listed position on these sites does not change season by season the way our own recorded statistics do.

                 & ~position_365["position_365scores"].isin(VALID_POSITIONS))

print(f"Dropped {int(not_a_player.sum())} non-player matches (Coach / General Manager)")

Dropped 27 non-player matches (Coach / General Manager)
365scores position resolved for 1341 of 2363 players

With both sources reduced to one row per player, we compared them directly. Wikipedia infoboxes can go stale or list a player's original amateur/draft position, while 365scores is a dedicated, actively maintained basketball database, so when both sources resolve a position and they disagree, we kept the 365scores value; when only one source resolves, we used whichever one did.

In [48]:
features = features.merge(wiki_lookup[["player_id", "position_wiki"]], on="player_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
features = features.merge(position_365, on="player_id", how="left", validate="m:1")

features["position_reconciled"] = features["position_365scores"].combine_first(features["position_wiki"])
features["position_reconciled_source"] = pd.Series(pd.NA, index=features.index, dtype="object")
features.loc[features["position_365scores"].notna(), "position_reconciled_source"] = "365scores"
features.loc[features["position_365scores"].isna() & features["position_wiki"].notna(),
             "position_reconciled_source"] = "wikipedia"

player_level = features.drop_duplicates("player_id")
both_resolved = player_level["position_365scores"].notna() & player_level["position_wiki"].notna()
disagree = both_resolved & (player_level["position_365scores"] != player_level["position_wiki"])

print(f"Players with both sources resolved: {int(both_resolved.sum())}")
print(f"Of those, sources disagree (365scores kept): {int(disagree.sum())}")
print(f"Players with a reconciled position overall: "
      f"{player_level['position_reconciled'].notna().sum()} of {len(player_level)}")

The reconciled five-category label covers 97.8% of the eligible sample -- higher coverage than the original position column itself (97.1%). Between the two external sources, we can resolve a position for some players whose EuroLeague biography page never listed one.

Checking the reconciled position against EuroLeague's own label¶

Since we now have a finer five-category label built from two outside sources, we checked it against EuroLeague's own three-category position -- the source we treat as authoritative for the coarse split, since it is the site the rest of this project's data comes from. We mapped Point Guard and Shooting Guard to Guard, Small Forward and Power Forward to Forward, and left Center unchanged, then compared the two labels for every player where both are available.

In [50]:

    "Point Guard": "Guard", "Shooting Guard": "Guard",
    "Small Forward": "Forward", "Power Forward": "Forward",
    "Center": "Center",
}
features["position_reconciled_3cat"] = features["position_reconciled"].map(CAT5_TO_3)

comparable = features.dropna(subset=["position", "position_reconciled_3cat"]).drop_duplicates("player_id")
agreement = (comparable["position"] == comparable["position_reconciled_3cat"]).mean()
print(f"Players comparable: {len(comparable)}")
print(f"Agreement with EuroLeague position: {agreement:.1%}")

                         rownames=["EuroLeague position"], colnames=["Reconciled (mapped to 3 categories)"])

The two labels agree for 79.2% of the 2,058 comparable players. The disagreement is concentrated where we would expect real ambiguity rather than a data problem: the two largest off-diagonal cells are Center-labeled-by-EuroLeague-but-Forward-by-reconciliation (141 players) and Forward-labeled-by-EuroLeague-but-Guard-by-reconciliation (121 players), which is consistent with combo/tweener players who get listed differently depending on the source. Only 17 players swap directly between Guard and Center, the two positions with the least basketball overlap. This supports treating position_reconciled as a genuine five-category refinement of the same underlying label rather than a different signal. We therefore use position_reconciled as our main reference label for interpreting the discovered roles, with the three-category position as a coarser supplementary comparison; neither is ever a clustering input.

Selecting the final clustering features¶

With a complete eligible sample, the next question was which of the candidate columns should define a player role. We wanted features that describe how a player contributes on the court -- shot volume, shooting efficiency, playmaking, rebounding, defense, physical profile, and shot location -- rather than general quality, playing time, or data coverage, and we did not want to give any single behavior extra weight by including several mathematical versions of it. Traditional position stays out of the model entirely. We started with shot location, which had the largest group of candidate variables.

Shot location¶

We had 17 spatial variables available: seven summaries calculated directly from the shot coordinates (mean lateral and longitudinal position, their standard deviations, and the mean, median, and standard deviation of raw shot distance) and ten shares of attempts in the recorded zones A-J. Entering all 17 as separate columns would give shot location far more weight in a distance-based clustering than any other feature group, simply because it has more columns, and the columns overlap heavily -- mean and median distance measure nearly the same thing, and the zone shares are built from the same shots as the coordinate summaries. One option was to compress the spatial block with its own PCA, fitted on the standardized values of the 4,568 eligible rows.

As a first test we fitted a five-component PCA to all 17 standardized variables and checked whether any component tracks the recording period rather than shooting behavior. For each component we measured the R² between an indicator for the two earliest seasons (E2007-E2008) and the component scores, i.e. the share of that component's score variance explained by the indicator.

In [52]:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

TABLE_DIR = REPO_ROOT / "outputs" / "tables"
EARLY_SEASONS = ["E2007", "E2008"]
COORDINATE_SPATIAL_FEATURES = [
    "mean_lateral_shot_position",
    "lateral_shot_position_std",
    "mean_longitudinal_shot_position",
    "longitudinal_shot_position_std",
    "mean_raw_shot_distance",
    "median_raw_shot_distance",
    "raw_shot_distance_std",
]
ZONE_SHARE_FEATURES = [f"zone_{letter}_attempt_share" for letter in "abcdefghij"]

eligible_spatial = features.loc[features["eligible_for_modeling"],
                                ["season_code"] + COORDINATE_SPATIAL_FEATURES + ZONE_SHARE_FEATURES]
is_early_row = eligible_spatial["season_code"].isin(EARLY_SEASONS).to_numpy()


def early_period_r2(scores, is_early):
    scores = pd.DataFrame(scores)
    period_means = scores.groupby(is_early).transform("mean")
    return (((period_means - scores.mean()) ** 2).sum() / ((scores - scores.mean()) ** 2).sum()).to_numpy()


all_spatial_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(
    eligible_spatial[COORDINATE_SPATIAL_FEATURES + ZONE_SHARE_FEATURES])
initial_pca = PCA(n_components=5, svd_solver="full").fit(all_spatial_scaled)
initial_scores = initial_pca.transform(all_spatial_scaled)

print(f"Eligible rows: {len(eligible_spatial)} ({int(is_early_row.sum())} from E2007-E2008)")
pd.DataFrame({
    "explained_variance_ratio": initial_pca.explained_variance_ratio_,
    "early_period_r2": early_period_r2(initial_scores, is_early_row),
    "mean_score_E2007_E2008": initial_scores[is_early_row].mean(axis=0),
    "mean_score_E2009_E2025": initial_scores[~is_early_row].mean(axis=0),
}, index=[f"pc{i}" for i in range(1, 6)]).round(3)

Eligible rows: 4568 (492 from E2007-E2008)

The second component of this initial PCA is mainly a recording-period indicator. The E2007-E2008 indicator explains 62.5% of the variance of its scores -- not 62.5% of the total spatial variance, of which this component carries 15.2% -- and the 492 early rows average +3.66 on it against -0.44 for the later seasons. The fourth component shows the same pattern more weakly (0.196). A change in playing style would not separate two seasons from the following seventeen this sharply, so we went back to the shot records and compared the coordinates, and the location of each zone letter, between the two periods.

In [53]:

    coord_x_p01=("coord_x", lambda s: s.quantile(0.01)),
    coord_x_median=("coord_x", "median"),

    valid_shots[is_three_point].groupby(shot_period[is_three_point])["raw_shot_distance"].median())

The coordinate frame appears compatible across the two periods. The median lateral position is 0 in both, the lateral range (1st to 99th percentile) is -683 to 687 in E2007-E2008 and -690 to 696 afterwards, and the longitudinal range starts at the same place (about -35). Together with the basket location at (0, 0) that we found earlier, this points to a stable origin and lateral scale. The shot distributions themselves are not identical: the 99th percentile of coord_y is 759 against 828, and the median three-point attempt is taken at 694 against 728 raw units. We therefore treat the coordinate summaries as usable across seasons, while the typical shot locations differ somewhat between eras.

The zone letters are not. From E2009 onward, A sits at the basket (median position (0, 6)), B and C are short-range shots on either side of it, D and E are mid-range, F and G are long two-pointers, H and I are three-pointers on each side, and J is a rare long-distance zone (593 attempts). In E2007-E2008 the same letters mark different places: A has a median position of (658, 143) and consists essentially of three-point attempts, H and I contain almost no three-pointers, and J holds 5,834 attempts, essentially all of them threes. The same letter therefore refers to a different area of the court depending on the season, which is what the second component of the initial PCA picked up.

We looked for an official definition of the zones. The Kaggle page for the dataset (https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/babissamothrakis/euroleague-datasets) states that the CSV files were generated from the official EuroLeague API, but it does not provide a map, boundary definitions, or a historical dictionary for zones A-J. An independent analysis by Georgios Giasemidis of shot data from the same official API (https://giasemidis.github.io/2022/11/06/euroleague-shots-data-errors.html) reports systematic inconsistencies in the recorded shot data, such as shots tagged as three-pointers that are located well inside the arc. That article supports the general point that the official shot records are not fully consistent, but it does not examine the A-J zone definitions or show that they changed; the evidence for that specific change is our own comparison above.

Because the zone definitions are undocumented and not consistent over time, we decided not to infer corrected historical zone labels. The ten zone shares stay in the feature table as descriptive and quality-control fields but are excluded from the clustering input, and we relied on the seven summaries calculated directly from the recorded coordinates. We first tested whether a PCA of these seven summaries would represent shot location better than the summaries themselves, standardizing them on the 4,568 eligible rows and keeping three components.

coordinate_scores = coordinate_pca.transform(spatial_scaler.transform(spatial_inputs))

print(pd.DataFrame({
    "explained_variance_ratio": coordinate_pca.explained_variance_ratio_,
    "cumulative": np.cumsum(coordinate_pca.explained_variance_ratio_),

}, index=["pc1", "pc2", "pc3"]).round(4).to_string(), "\n")

Three components keep 93.6% of the variance of the seven coordinate summaries (69.2%, 14.3%, and 10.1%), and none of them tracks the recording period (the largest early-period R² is 0.006). But the second component is almost entirely mean_lateral_shot_position (loading 0.999) -- which side of the court a player shoots from on average -- and shooting from the left or the right is not in itself a player role. With only seven candidate variables, the reduction in dimensionality was too small to justify replacing understandable variables with abstract components. Instead, we chose a few of the original summaries directly, using their correlations to avoid keeping two versions of the same information.

The correlations support a smaller set of original summaries:

  • mean_raw_shot_distance and median_raw_shot_distance correlate at 0.924. We kept the median, the player's typical shooting range, because it is less sensitive to a few extreme shots than the mean.
  • mean_longitudinal_shot_position correlates at 0.923 with mean distance and 0.850 with median distance, so it mostly repeats shooting range. We excluded it.
  • longitudinal_shot_position_std correlates at 0.882 with raw_shot_distance_std. We kept raw_shot_distance_std, the variation in shooting distance, and excluded the longitudinal spread.
  • lateral_shot_position_std measures how widely a player's shots are spread across the court. It correlates at 0.826 with the median distance -- players who shoot from farther out also spread wider along the arc -- but it describes width rather than depth, so we kept it.
  • mean_lateral_shot_position is almost unrelated to everything else (0.034 to 0.048). It only says which side of the court a player favors, so we excluded it.

The shot-location profile in the model is therefore median_raw_shot_distance, raw_shot_distance_std, and lateral_shot_position_std. The other four coordinate summaries, the ten zone shares, and the PCA components are not clustering inputs.

Other candidate features¶

The remaining candidates raised four questions. points_per_40 might only repeat shooting volume and efficiency, which we already represent separately. Free-throw attempts per 40, the free-throw attempt rate, and fouls received per 40 might measure the same contact pressure three times. The two-point and three-point attempt shares, and their event-based versions, might duplicate each other. Finally, fouls committed might partly reflect playing time rather than role. We checked each of these on the eligible sample.

In [56]:
candidates = features.loc[features["eligible_for_modeling"]]
minutes_per_game = candidates["minutes"] / candidates["games_played"]
points_rebuilt_per_40 = (
    2 * candidates["two_points_attempted"] * candidates["two_points_percentage"]
    + 3 * candidates["three_points_attempted"] * candidates["three_points_percentage"]
    + candidates["free_throws_attempted"] * candidates["free_throws_percentage"]
) / candidates["minutes"] * REGULATION_GAME_MINUTES


def r(a, b):
    return np.corrcoef(a, b)[0, 1]


overlap_checks = pd.Series({
    "r(points_per_40, points rebuilt from attempts and percentages)":
        r(candidates["points_per_40"], points_rebuilt_per_40),
    "r(two_point_attempt_share, three_point_attempt_share)":
        r(candidates["two_point_attempt_share"], candidates["three_point_attempt_share"]),
    "max |event_three_point_attempt_share - three_point_attempt_share|":
        (candidates["event_three_point_attempt_share"] - candidates["three_point_attempt_share"]).abs().max(),
    "r(fouls_received_per_40, free_throw_attempts_per_40)":
        r(candidates["fouls_received_per_40"], candidates["free_throw_attempts_per_40"]),
    "r(fouls_received_per_40, free_throw_attempt_rate)":
        r(candidates["fouls_received_per_40"], candidates["free_throw_attempt_rate"]),
    "r(free_throw_attempts_per_40, free_throw_attempt_rate)":
        r(candidates["free_throw_attempts_per_40"], candidates["free_throw_attempt_rate"]),
    "r(fouls_committed_per_40, fouls_received_per_40)":
        r(candidates["fouls_committed_per_40"], candidates["fouls_received_per_40"]),
})
print(overlap_checks.round(3).to_string(), "\n")

blocks_per_40                 -0.129
defensive_rebounds_per_40     -0.001
steals_per_40                  0.132
turnovers_per_40               0.133
two_point_attempts_per_40      0.165
three_point_attempts_per_40    0.196
free_throw_attempts_per_40     0.208
fouls_received_per_40          0.241
assists_per_40                 0.248
points_per_40                  0.363
dtype: float64
  • Points. points_per_40 is almost exactly rebuilt from attempts and shooting percentages (r = 1.000; the percentages are rounded to three decimals in the source file), so it is an outcome of volume and efficiency rather than a separate behavior. We excluded it and kept its components.
  • Contact pressure. Fouls received per 40 correlates at 0.871 with free-throw attempts per 40 and at 0.694 with the free-throw attempt rate, and the two free-throw measures correlate at 0.847 with each other. We kept one measure, fouls_received_per_40, because it counts every foul a player draws rather than only those that lead to free throws, and excluded the two free-throw volume measures. free_throws_percentage stays as the free-throw efficiency measure. As a consequence, the 34 eligible rows without a free-throw attempt carry a neutral value for that percentage and give the model no explicit zero-attempt signal -- unlike three-pointers, where the selected three_point_attempts_per_40 is zero. We did not add has_free_throw_attempts or another free-throw-volume feature to compensate: a rare binary flag would be one more representation of contact pressure, and the choice affects only 34 of the 4,568 eligible rows.
  • Attempt shares. The two-point and three-point attempt shares are exact complements (r = -1.000), and the event-based shares differ from the season-level shares by at most 0.001. Shot selection is already represented by the two per-40 attempt rates and the shot-location profile, so we excluded all four shares.
  • Fouls committed and fouls received. The two correlate at only 0.010, so they are not interchangeable. Fouls committed can reflect defensive physicality, aggressive or interior defensive responsibility, and the cost of a player's defensive involvement; fouls received can reflect offensive pressure -- ball handling, attacks on the rim, and post play that force defensive contact. We kept both, because they may separate roles that scoring and efficiency features do not capture. fouls_committed_per_40 has the strongest relationship with minutes per game of any per-40 rate (r = -0.570): players with shorter stints commit fouls at a higher rate per minute. We still kept it: the relationship is moderate rather than an exact duplication (r² of about 0.32), the rate can still carry genuine role information, and the eligibility rule of at least 5 games and 100 minutes already removes the least stable small-sample rates.

The remaining exclusions follow directly from the goal of describing role rather than quality, playing time, or data coverage, and are listed with the full decision below.

The strongest correlation is 0.826, between median_raw_shot_distance and lateral_shot_position_std, followed by three-point attempts per 40 with median distance (0.816) and with lateral spread (0.757). These reflect a real basketball pattern -- perimeter shooters take more threes, from farther out and across a wider part of the arc -- rather than two versions of the same measurement, and no pair comes close to an exact duplicate. The rebounding rates and height are related in the expected direction (0.687 and 0.667), but height is a physical attribute and rebounding a responsibility, so both stay. These 17 features are our final clustering feature set.

Preparing the modeling matrix¶

Before clustering, two properties of the selected features needed attention: how reliable the shooting percentages are, and the very different scales of the 17 features.

Stabilizing shooting percentages from few attempts¶

A shooting percentage is an estimate of how well a player converts a shot type, and that estimate is only as good as the number of attempts behind it. Many eligible rows have very few attempts of a given type -- a forward who took one three-pointer all season is recorded at either 0% or 100%. Those values say almost nothing about the player's shooting, but after standardization they would be among the most extreme values in the whole matrix and could pull a player toward a cluster for no basketball reason.

We therefore replaced each of the three percentages in the modeling matrix with an attempt-weighted shrinkage estimate,

adjusted_percentage = (makes + k * prior_mean) / (attempts + k), with k = 10,

where prior_mean is the attempt-weighted shooting percentage for that shot type across the eligible rows. This works like adding ten attempts at the sample's average rate: the prior carries a weight of 10/11 for a player with one attempt, one half at ten attempts, and less than one tenth beyond 90 attempts, so high-volume shooters keep almost exactly their observed percentage. A row with no attempts receives the prior mean, which keeps the earlier distinction between a genuine 0% and an undefined percentage. To check that the adjustment addresses the problem, we counted the rows more than three standard deviations from the mean of each percentage before and after it, and how many of them rest on 1-9 attempts.

In [61]:
SHOOTING_PERCENTAGE_COUNTS = {
    "two_points_percentage": ("two_points_made", "two_points_attempted"),
    "three_points_percentage": ("three_points_made", "three_points_attempted"),
    "free_throws_percentage": ("free_throws_made", "free_throws_attempted"),
}
SHRINKAGE_K = 10

modeling_rows = features.loc[features["eligible_for_modeling"]]
modeling_features = modeling_rows[FINAL_CLUSTERING_FEATURES].copy()


def is_extreme(values):
    return ((values - values.mean()) / values.std(ddof=0)).abs() > 3


shrinkage_check = []
for pct_col, (made_col, attempted_col) in SHOOTING_PERCENTAGE_COUNTS.items():
    made, attempted = modeling_rows[made_col], modeling_rows[attempted_col]
    prior_mean = made.sum() / attempted.sum()
    modeling_features[pct_col] = (made + SHRINKAGE_K * prior_mean) / (attempted + SHRINKAGE_K)

    few_attempts = attempted.between(1, 9)
    extreme_observed = is_extreme(modeling_rows[pct_col])
    extreme_adjusted = is_extreme(modeling_features[pct_col])
    shrinkage_check.append({
        "feature": pct_col,
        "prior_mean": round(prior_mean, 3),
        "rows_with_1_9_attempts": int(few_attempts.sum()),
        "observed_abs_z_over_3": int(extreme_observed.sum()),
        "observed_of_which_1_9_attempts": int((extreme_observed & few_attempts).sum()),
        "adjusted_abs_z_over_3": int(extreme_adjusted.sum()),
        "adjusted_of_which_1_9_attempts": int((extreme_adjusted & few_attempts).sum()),
    })

pd.DataFrame(shrinkage_check).set_index("feature")

In the observed percentages, the extreme values were mostly small samples: 25 of the 26 extreme three-point percentages and 25 of the 33 extreme free-throw percentages came from rows with 1-9 attempts, and so did 17 of the 42 extreme two-point percentages. After the adjustment, only one extreme value across the three features still rests on fewer than ten attempts. The extremes that remain belong to players with enough attempts for them to reflect real shooting differences, which is the information we included shooting efficiency for. We chose k = 10 because the noisy extremes were concentrated below about ten attempts; a much larger value would also start to flatten genuine differences between players with a moderate number of attempts.

The three percentage columns of the modeling matrix keep their names but hold these adjusted estimates; the feature table itself still keeps the observed percentages. The other 14 features keep the representation chosen in the feature selection.

Scaling the features¶

The 17 features are measured in very different units: height in centimeters (standard deviation 8.6), shooting percentages as proportions, per-40 rates (standard deviations 0.59-3.15), and the shot-location summaries in raw coordinate units (58-217). K-Means and GMM compare players through distances in feature space, so on these raw scales median_raw_shot_distance would dominate the distances simply because its numbers are larger, while a real difference in shooting percentage would barely count. We therefore standardized every feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 on the 4,568 eligible rows, so that each feature enters the clustering on the same scale.

Apart from the shooting adjustment, we did not transform any feature. Several are skewed, most clearly blocks_per_40 and assists_per_40, but those long tails come from a minority of players -- shot-blocking bigs and primary ball handlers -- whose unusual values are exactly the kind of role difference we want the clustering to find. Compressing them with a log or similar transformation would have no substantive justification, and no player is removed for being unusual.

In [62]:

X_scaled = pd.DataFrame(feature_scaler.fit_transform(modeling_features),
                        index=modeling_rows.index, columns=FINAL_CLUSTERING_FEATURES)

feature_decisions.loc[feature_decisions["feature_group"] == "Shooting efficiency",
                      ["final_representation", "reason"]] = [
    "attempt-weighted shrinkage toward the eligible-sample mean (k = 10)",
    "Conversion of each shot type, stabilized so that percentages from very few attempts "
    "do not become extreme; zero-attempt rows receive the attempt-weighted mean."]
feature_decisions.to_csv(TABLE_DIR / "final_clustering_feature_decisions.csv", index=False)

Exploring the structure of the modeling matrix with PCA¶

Before clustering, we wanted to see what the standardized 17-feature space looks like: how many independent directions of variation it really has, which basketball characteristics drive the largest differences between player-season-team observations, and whether the observations already fall into visibly separate groups. We fitted a PCA with all 17 components to X_scaled, so the components describe exactly the matrix the clustering will use.

In [63]:
modeling_pca = PCA(svd_solver="full").fit(X_scaled)
pca_scores = modeling_pca.transform(X_scaled)
component_labels = [f"PC{i}" for i in range(1, len(FINAL_CLUSTERING_FEATURES) + 1)]

explained_variance = pd.DataFrame({
    "eigenvalue": modeling_pca.explained_variance_,
    "explained_variance_ratio": modeling_pca.explained_variance_ratio_,
    "cumulative": np.cumsum(modeling_pca.explained_variance_ratio_),
}, index=component_labels)
print(explained_variance.T.round(3).to_string())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))

The first component is clearly dominant: it carries 38.1% of the total variance (eigenvalue 6.48, as much as six and a half of the original standardized features). The second adds 13.3% and the third 7.2%, so the first two together keep 51.5% and the first three 58.7%. After that the curve flattens: PC4 to PC10 each explain between 3.1% and 6.1%, there is no clear point where the remaining components become negligible, and eight components are needed to pass 80%. The playing-style space therefore has one strong main axis and one clear secondary axis, but about 41% of the variation lies beyond PC3, spread over many smaller directions.

To see which characteristics define the leading components, we looked at the correlation between each feature and the scores of the first three components, together with the share of each feature's variance that the PC1-PC2 plane keeps.
