PC1 is an interior-to-perimeter axis. On the negative side are offensive rebounds (-0.86), height (-0.76), blocks (-0.73), defensive rebounds (-0.69), two-point attempts (-0.66), and two-point percentage (-0.51); on the positive side are lateral spread of shots (0.87), median shot distance (0.85), three-point attempts (0.84), variation in shot distance (0.69), free-throw percentage (0.52), and assists (0.49). A low PC1 score describes a tall player who shoots close to the basket, rebounds, and blocks shots; a high score describes a player who shoots from range, across the width of the court, and passes more.

PC2 is mainly on-ball offensive involvement. It is driven by turnovers (0.80), fouls received (0.67), assists (0.65), and two-point attempts (0.48), with height (-0.36) and lateral spread (-0.34) mildly negative. A high PC2 score describes a player who handles the ball, creates, attacks the basket, and draws fouls -- a difference that exists alongside the interior-perimeter split of PC1 rather than repeating it.

PC3 is weaker and mixed. Its largest correlations are three-point percentage (0.58), fouls committed (-0.50), free-throw percentage (0.47), and steals (-0.38). It contrasts shooting accuracy with defensive fouling and activity, but with 7.2% of the variance and no dominant feature, we read it as a secondary contrast rather than a role dimension of its own.

The last column shows what a two-dimensional view leaves out. The PC1-PC2 plane keeps between 0.49 and 0.87 of the variance of the shot-volume, shot-location, rebounding, playmaking, fouls-received, height, and blocks features, but only 0.04 of three-point percentage, 0.10 of steals, 0.18 of fouls committed, and 0.28 of two-point and free-throw percentage. Shooting efficiency and part of the defensive activity therefore lie largely outside the plane we can plot.

The projection does not show clearly separated groups. Along PC1 the density is uneven: a dense peak of perimeter-oriented observations on the positive side, a broad and flatter band of interior-oriented observations on the negative side, and somewhat lower density between them -- but that region is still populated, so players of every intermediate profile exist. Along PC2 the observations form a single spread, slightly longer on the side of high on-ball involvement, without any visible split.

We therefore read the structure as overlapping regions of different density within a continuous spectrum of playing styles, not as naturally isolated groups. The plot cannot tell us how many roles exist: it shows 51.5% of the variance, and some role differences, such as shooting efficiency and defensive activity, lie mostly in the directions it leaves out. It does indicate that the clusters will divide dense, connected regions of the feature space rather than separate isolated groups, so how firmly observations are assigned to their cluster will matter when we evaluate the models.

Using PCA for exploration, not as the clustering input¶

We decided to keep PCA as an exploratory and visualization tool and to fit K-Means and GMM on the original 17 standardized features. The results above give three reasons. First, the variance is not concentrated in a few components: beyond PC3, no component explains more than 6.1% and there is no natural cut-off, so any truncation would be an arbitrary choice that discards a substantial share of the information -- 41% with three components and still 17% with eight. Second, what would be discarded is not noise: three-point percentage, steals, fouls committed, and two-point and free-throw percentage are mostly represented outside the leading components, and we selected these features deliberately as parts of a player's role. Third, the 17 features are already a curated set without near-duplicates, and 17 dimensions for 4,568 observations do not require reduction for K-Means or GMM. Clustering on the original features also lets us describe every cluster directly in basketball terms.

A K-Means baseline¶

As a first clustering model, and as a baseline for the Gaussian mixture models, we fitted K-Means to the 17 standardized features in X_scaled for every number of clusters from 2 to 12. Each fit keeps the best of 20 random initializations, which reduces the chance that a solution reflects an unlucky starting point. For each solution we recorded the inertia (the total squared distance of the observations to their cluster centers), the silhouette score computed on all 4,568 observations, and the sizes of the smallest and largest clusters.

In [66]:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

KMEANS_K_RANGE = range(2, 13)

kmeans_models = {}
kmeans_rows = []
for k in KMEANS_K_RANGE:
    model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=20, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_scaled)
    kmeans_models[k] = model
    cluster_sizes = np.bincount(model.labels_)
    kmeans_rows.append({
        "k": k,
        "inertia": model.inertia_,
        "silhouette": silhouette_score(X_scaled, model.labels_),
        "smallest_cluster": cluster_sizes.min(),
        "largest_cluster": cluster_sizes.max(),
        "smallest_cluster_share": cluster_sizes.min() / len(X_scaled),
    })

kmeans_comparison = pd.DataFrame(kmeans_rows).set_index("k")
kmeans_comparison["inertia_reduction"] = -kmeans_comparison["inertia"].diff()
print(kmeans_comparison.round({"inertia": 0, "inertia_reduction": 0, "silhouette": 3,
                               "smallest_cluster_share": 3}).to_string())

Neither diagnostic points to a sharp optimum. The inertia curve bends gradually rather than at one clear elbow: adding a third cluster reduces inertia by 6,490 and a fourth by 3,856, but the fifth adds only 1,746, and from there each additional cluster reduces it by between 1,468 and 595. Most of the gain from splitting the data is therefore achieved by k = 4, with diminishing returns afterwards.

The silhouette score is highest at k = 2 (0.299) and then declines almost steadily, from 0.175 at k = 3 and 0.148 at k = 4 to between 0.081 and 0.098 from k = 7 on. Values this low mean that many observations lie nearly as close to a neighboring cluster as to their own, which is what the continuous PC1-PC2 projection led us to expect: K-Means is dividing connected regions of the feature space rather than finding isolated groups. Because the score falls with every added cluster, it can rank k = 2 above everything else but does not identify a preferred number of clusters beyond that.

We looked at cluster sizes only to detect degenerate or suspiciously small clusters, not as a criterion in itself: there is no reason to expect basketball roles to be equally common, so a valid solution may well contain clusters of very different sizes. None of the solutions shows such a problem. Even at k = 12 the smallest cluster still holds 300 observations (6.6% of the sample).

The k = 2 solution has the highest silhouette, and it is a valid partition of the data, but it mainly captures the broad interior-perimeter distinction we saw along PC1: one cluster of 1,226 observations has a mean PC1 score of -3.68, the interior side, and the other, with 3,342 observations, a mean of 1.35. It describes the one contrast that already dominates the PCA, so it says little about how playing styles differ beyond that broad division, which is what our research question is about.

We selected k = 4 as a practical K-Means baseline, mainly because it is where the inertia curve starts to flatten: the fifth cluster reduces inertia by less than half as much as the fourth. The support for it is modest. The elbow is gradual, the silhouette declines almost steadily as clusters are added (0.148 at k = 4), k = 5 is a similarly reasonable alternative (silhouette 0.134), and the low silhouette values throughout show that no K-Means solution here describes strongly separated groups. The baseline is therefore a reference solution for comparing models, not an estimate of how many player roles exist. K-Means assumes roughly spherical clusters of similar spread, and inertia and silhouette are not comparable with the likelihood-based criteria used for Gaussian mixture models, so the number of clusters in the final model is chosen separately, from the evidence for that model.

Gaussian mixture models¶

K-Means assigns every observation to exactly one cluster and, because it measures plain Euclidean distance to the cluster centers, implicitly treats every cluster as a round group with the same spread. A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) instead describes the data as a mixture of multivariate normal components, each with its own mean and covariance matrix, and gives every observation a probability of belonging to each component. We used full covariance matrices, because different basketball roles may differ not only in their typical values but also in how much their features vary and how those features move together. To compare numbers of components we used the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), which rewards the likelihood of the data but penalizes every additional parameter; a lower BIC indicates a better balance between fit and complexity.

We first fitted full-covariance models for k = 2 to 12 with the library's default covariance regularization, reg_covar = 1e-6 -- a tiny constant added to the diagonal of every covariance matrix for numerical stability -- keeping the best of 10 initializations for each k. Next to BIC we recorded the smallest variance of any component in any direction: the smallest eigenvalue of a component's covariance matrix, minus the regularization constant. A value near zero means that a component has no spread at all in some direction of the feature space.

In [68]:
import warnings

from sklearn.exceptions import ConvergenceWarning
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture

GMM_K_RANGE = range(2, 13)
COLLAPSE_THRESHOLD = 1e-4


def fit_gmm_sweep(reg_covar):
    models, rows = {}, []
    for k in GMM_K_RANGE:
        with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
            warnings.simplefilter("always", ConvergenceWarning)
            model = GaussianMixture(n_components=k, covariance_type="full", reg_covar=reg_covar,
                                    n_init=10, max_iter=500, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_scaled)
        hard_counts = np.bincount(model.predict(X_scaled), minlength=k)
        models[k] = model
        rows.append({
            "k": k,
            "bic": model.bic(X_scaled),
            "converged": model.converged_,
            "convergence_warnings": len(caught),
            "smallest_within_component_variance":
                min(np.linalg.eigvalsh(cov).min() for cov in model.covariances_) - reg_covar,
            "smallest_weight": model.weights_.min(),
            "smallest_hard_count": hard_counts.min(),
            "mean_max_posterior": model.predict_proba(X_scaled).max(axis=1).mean(),
        })
    summary = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("k")
    summary["delta_bic"] = summary["bic"] - summary["bic"].min()
    return models, summary


default_gmm_models, default_gmm_summary = fit_gmm_sweep(reg_covar=1e-6)
print(default_gmm_summary[["bic", "delta_bic", "converged", "convergence_warnings",
                           "smallest_within_component_variance"]]
      .to_string(formatters={"bic": "{:,.0f}".format, "delta_bic": "{:,.0f}".format,
                             "smallest_within_component_variance": "{:.1e}".format}))

       bic delta_bic  converged  convergence_warnings smallest_within_component_variance

Taken at face value, BIC favors a fairly detailed solution: the lowest value is at k = 10, with k = 9 only 108 higher, and every fit converged without a warning. The path to that minimum is irregular, though. The largest single drop comes from four to five components (from 154,726 to 147,246), and another large one from eight to nine. The last column shows what changes at k = 5: from there on, every solution contains a component whose smallest variance is zero up to rounding error (of the order of 1e-16), which is not the case for two to four components. We inspected the components of the k = 10 solution that behave this way.

zero_three_point_attempts = modeling_rows["three_points_attempted"].eq(0).to_numpy()
zero_blocks = modeling_rows["blocks_favour"].eq(0).to_numpy()
print(f"Eligible rows with zero three-point attempts: {zero_three_point_attempts.sum()}")
print(f"Eligible rows with zero blocks: {zero_blocks.sum()}\n")

default_best_k = default_gmm_summary["bic"].idxmin()
default_best_model = default_gmm_models[default_best_k]
default_best_labels = default_best_model.predict(X_scaled)

collapsed_rows = []
for component, cov in enumerate(default_best_model.covariances_):
    within_variances = np.linalg.eigvalsh(cov) - default_best_model.reg_covar
    if within_variances.min() < COLLAPSE_THRESHOLD:
        feature_variances = pd.Series(np.diag(cov) - default_best_model.reg_covar,
                                      index=FINAL_CLUSTERING_FEATURES)
        in_component = default_best_labels == component
        collapsed_rows.append({
            "component": component,
            "hard_count": int(in_component.sum()),
            "collapsed_directions": int((within_variances < COLLAPSE_THRESHOLD).sum()),
            "zero_variance_features": ", ".join(
                feature_variances.index[feature_variances < COLLAPSE_THRESHOLD]),
            "share_zero_three_point_attempts": zero_three_point_attempts[in_component].mean(),
            "share_zero_blocks": zero_blocks[in_component].mean(),
        })

print(f"Collapsed components in the default-regularization solution with k = {default_best_k}:")
with pd.option_context("display.max_colwidth", None):
    display(pd.DataFrame(collapsed_rows).set_index("component").round(3))

Two components of the k = 10 solution have collapsed. The first consists of exactly the 443 eligible observations without a three-point attempt. Within it, three_point_attempts_per_40 is 0 for every row and the shrinkage-adjusted three_points_percentage is the prior mean for every row, since zero attempts receive the prior, so the component has no variance in either feature. The second consists of 865 observations that all have zero blocks -- most of the 933 eligible observations without a block -- and has no variance in blocks_per_40.

These zero values are legitimate basketball data: some players never attempt a three-pointer, and many go a whole season without blocking a shot. The problem is not the data or the preprocessing but the way a continuous Gaussian model treats a large group of identical values. As the variance of a normal component shrinks toward zero in one direction, its density at that exact value grows without bound, so a component that captures such a point mass can raise the likelihood almost arbitrarily; with reg_covar = 1e-6, nothing stops the variance from falling to practically zero. BIC rewards that likelihood gain, so part of the advantage of the solutions with five or more components comes from this covariance collapse rather than from additional structure in how players play. A lower BIC therefore does not mean that these solutions describe more meaningful roles, and the absence of convergence warnings does not reveal the problem, because the algorithm converges correctly to a degenerate solution.

We therefore tested whether stronger regularization would prevent the collapse without restricting the model more than necessary. reg_covar adds a constant to the diagonal of every component covariance matrix. Every estimated variance is shifted up by that constant -- so none can fall below it -- and variances that were already large are inflated slightly as well. Since the features are standardized to unit variance, 0.01 corresponds to 1% of a feature's overall variance and 0.1 to 10%. We repeated the full sweep with both values. Absolute BIC values are not comparable across settings, because the regularization changes the fitted models themselves, so we compared how the settings behave: which solutions BIC prefers and whether any component still collapses.

In [70]:
gmm_models = {1e-6: default_gmm_models}
gmm_summaries = {1e-6: default_gmm_summary}
for reg_covar in [0.01, 0.1]:
    gmm_models[reg_covar], gmm_summaries[reg_covar] = fit_gmm_sweep(reg_covar)

regularization_rows = []
for reg_covar, summary in gmm_summaries.items():
    ranked = summary["bic"].sort_values()
    leading = ranked.index[:2]
    regularization_rows.append({
        "reg_covar": reg_covar,
        "lowest_bic_k": leading[0],
        "second_lowest_bic_k": leading[1],
        "bic_gap_between_them": ranked.iloc[1] - ranked.iloc[0],
        "smallest_within_variance_in_leading_two":
            summary.loc[leading, "smallest_within_component_variance"].min(),
        "k_values_with_collapsed_component":
            ", ".join(str(k) for k in summary.index[
                summary["smallest_within_component_variance"] < COLLAPSE_THRESHOLD]) or "none",
    })

pd.DataFrame(regularization_rows).set_index("reg_covar").style.format({
    "bic_gap_between_them": "{:,.0f}", "smallest_within_variance_in_leading_two": "{:.1e}"})

With either stronger setting, no solution between k = 2 and 12 contains a collapsed component; the smallest within-component variance in the two leading solutions is about 0.003 with reg_covar = 0.01 and 0.007 with 0.1, against zero under the default. The preferred number of components changes as well. Instead of k = 10 and 9, BIC now prefers k = 5 under both settings; only the runner-up differs, k = 6 (23 higher) with 0.01 and k = 4 (12 higher) with 0.1. The selected k is therefore the same under both non-degenerate settings, although the conclusions below remain conditional on the regularization we chose.

We kept reg_covar = 0.01. It is the smaller of the two stronger settings we tested and already prevents the collapse we observed. Compared with 0.1, it shifts every estimated variance by a smaller amount, so the components keep more freedom to represent genuine differences in spread and correlation between roles. Our aim was to remove a demonstrated numerical artifact, not to smooth the model further. We do not claim that 0.01 is the smallest value that would work, that it is optimal, or that it leaves the clustering unaffected: the regularization is a modeling assumption, and it cannot rule out every other kind of artifact. The remaining analysis uses the full-covariance models with reg_covar = 0.01 that were fitted for this comparison.

Under this specification, the BIC curve has a clear basin. It falls steeply up to k = 4, reaches its minimum at k = 5 (155,866), and k = 6 is almost level with it, only 23 higher; from k = 7 it rises steadily, to 3,741 above the minimum at k = 12, so there was no reason to extend the range. k = 4 is 884 above the minimum. All fits converged. The smallest within-component variance stays at about 0.003 up to k = 10 and falls to 0.0009 and 0.0002 at k = 11 and 12 -- still above our collapse threshold, but a sign that the largest solutions again start to concentrate a component on nearly identical values. None of the leading solutions shows this.

We selected k = 5. It has the lowest BIC, and it is also the lowest-BIC solution under the stronger 0.1 setting. By the usual convention, a BIC difference above 10 counts as strong evidence, so the margin of 23 over k = 6 favors five components. It is still a modest margin that holds under a stated regularization assumption, so k = 6 remains a close competing solution.

The five components have weights between 0.140 and 0.246. The hard assignments, which place each observation in its most probable component, give similar shares, from 620 to 1,162 observations. No component is small or degenerate; we report the sizes only for that reason, since roles need not be equally common. Most observations are assigned confidently -- 77.1% have a largest membership probability of at least 0.9, and only 3.5% have less than 0.6 -- although component 2 has a lower mean certainty (0.881) than the others, so its observations overlap more with neighboring components. Given the continuous structure in the PCA projection, some overlap of this kind is expected rather than a sign of failure.

BIC and K-Means inertia are not comparable model-selection criteria: BIC is not defined for K-Means, and inertia is the quantity K-Means itself minimizes. A distance-based measure such as the silhouette could be computed for both partitions, but it rewards compact, well-separated groups, which is what K-Means optimizes, so we did not use it to rank the two models. Instead we compared the partitions themselves with the adjusted Rand index, which measures how far two partitions agree, not which one is better. With the number of clusters held at four, K-Means and the GMM agree only moderately (adjusted Rand index 0.513), so changing the model alone already reassigns a substantial part of the sample. The selected five-component GMM agrees with the K-Means baseline at 0.409. The cross-tabulation shows that this is not one K-Means cluster split in two: GMM component 1 almost coincides with K-Means cluster 3 (748 of its 756 observations), while the other three K-Means clusters are redistributed across several components.

We selected the full-covariance GMM with five components and reg_covar = 0.01 as our clustering model. We chose it over the K-Means baseline not because flexible covariances or soft assignments are better by definition, but because it provides a likelihood-based criterion for the number of components, whose minimum was clearer than anything the K-Means diagnostics showed, and because its membership probabilities show how firmly each observation belongs to its component in a feature space where groups overlap. This does not establish that the GMM partition is better than the K-Means one. The choice is conditional on the regularization, k = 6 is a close alternative, and whether the five components are stable and correspond to meaningful basketball roles is not settled by the selection itself.

Checking the robustness of the five-component GMM¶

The five-component solution raised two practical questions before we could rely on it for interpretation: whether the component assignments depend on the random initialization of the EM algorithm, and whether they depend on including the lowest-participation rows in the eligible sample. We checked both, and then whether the E2007-E2008 recording-period difference we found when comparing coordinate systems shows up as a GMM component.

Stability under different random initializations¶

GaussianMixture already keeps the best of 10 initializations for a single call, but all of those initializations are drawn from the same random_state. To see whether a different draw of starting points would have landed on a different partition, we refit the selected specification -- five components, full covariance, reg_covar = 0.01 -- nine more times, each with its own random_state and again the best of 10 initializations, and compared every run to the original (random_state = 42) and to each other. Because a GMM's component numbering is arbitrary, we used the adjusted Rand index (ARI), which is invariant to relabeling, and also matched each run's components to the original with the Hungarian algorithm on their confusion matrix, to see what share of observations land in the same matched component.

In [73]:
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment


def match_components(reference_labels, other_labels, k):
    reference_labels = np.asarray(reference_labels)
    confusion = pd.crosstab(pd.Series(reference_labels), pd.Series(other_labels)).reindex(
        index=range(k), columns=range(k), fill_value=0).to_numpy()
    row_ind, col_ind = linear_sum_assignment(-confusion)
    mapping = dict(zip(col_ind, row_ind))
    aligned = pd.Series(other_labels).map(mapping).to_numpy()
    agreement = (aligned == reference_labels).mean()
    return mapping, agreement


STABILITY_SEEDS = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]

stability_models = {RANDOM_STATE: gmm_selected}
for seed in STABILITY_SEEDS:
    stability_models[seed] = GaussianMixture(n_components=GMM_SELECTED_K, covariance_type="full",
                                             reg_covar=GMM_REG_COVAR, n_init=10, max_iter=500,
                                             random_state=seed).fit(X_scaled)

stability_labels = {seed: model.predict(X_scaled) for seed, model in stability_models.items()}
seeds_all = [RANDOM_STATE] + STABILITY_SEEDS

ari_matrix = pd.DataFrame(
    [[adjusted_rand_score(stability_labels[a], stability_labels[b]) for b in seeds_all] for a in seeds_all],
    index=seeds_all, columns=seeds_all)
off_diagonal = ari_matrix.to_numpy()[~np.eye(len(seeds_all), dtype=bool)]

stability_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "bic": [stability_models[s].bic(X_scaled) for s in seeds_all],
    "ari_vs_random_state_42": [adjusted_rand_score(gmm_labels, stability_labels[s]) for s in seeds_all],
    "matched_agreement_vs_random_state_42": [
        match_components(gmm_labels.to_numpy(), stability_labels[s], GMM_SELECTED_K)[1]
        for s in seeds_all],
}, index=pd.Index(seeds_all, name="random_state")).round(3)

print(stability_summary.to_string(), "\n")
print(f"Pairwise ARI across all {len(seeds_all)} runs (including random_state = 42): "

Across the ten runs (random_state = 42 and nine others), BIC varies only from 155,864 to 155,885 -- effectively the same optimum, reached repeatedly rather than depending on one lucky draw. Component labels are similarly stable: the adjusted Rand index between any two of the ten runs averages 0.978 and is never below 0.929, and after matching each run's components to the original with the Hungarian algorithm, every run keeps at least 96.8% of observations in the same matched component (99.6% for most seeds; random_state = 8 is the least similar run at 96.8%). The five-component partition is therefore a stable property of the specification, not an artifact of the particular initialization behind random_state = 42.

Rerunning on the stricter 10 games / 200 minutes sample¶

When we selected the eligible sample, we kept 10 games / 200 minutes in reserve: a stricter participation rule that retains 3,679 of the 6,307 player-season-team rows, all of them already inside the 4,568-row eligible sample. We rebuilt the modeling matrix for exactly this stricter sample -- recomputing the shrinkage prior for the three shooting percentages and refitting StandardScaler on these rows only, the same procedure used for the full sample, just on fewer rows -- and fit the same specification used for the main result. We then compared its component labels with the original model's labels on the 3,679 rows they share, again using the adjusted Rand index and Hungarian matching, and checked a narrow band of nearby k on the stricter sample to confirm five components is still reasonable there.

In [74]:
STRICT_MIN_GAMES, STRICT_MIN_MINUTES = 10, 200
strict_mask = (features["games_played"] >= STRICT_MIN_GAMES) & (features["minutes"] >= STRICT_MIN_MINUTES)

print(f"Strict sample (10 games / 200 minutes): {len(strict_rows)} rows, "
      f"all inside the eligible sample: "
      f"{bool((strict_mask & ~features['eligible_for_modeling']).sum() == 0)}")

strict_modeling_features = strict_rows[FINAL_CLUSTERING_FEATURES].copy()
for pct_col, (made_col, attempted_col) in SHOOTING_PERCENTAGE_COUNTS.items():
    made, attempted = strict_rows[made_col], strict_rows[attempted_col]
    prior_mean = made.sum() / attempted.sum()
    strict_modeling_features[pct_col] = (made + SHRINKAGE_K * prior_mean) / (attempted + SHRINKAGE_K)

X_strict_scaled = pd.DataFrame(StandardScaler().fit_transform(strict_modeling_features),
                               index=strict_rows.index, columns=FINAL_CLUSTERING_FEATURES)

The stricter sample reproduces the same structure. Its own BIC is also minimized at five components (124,041, against 124,691 at four and 124,569 at six) -- the same ordering as on the full eligible sample. Restricting the original model's labels to the 3,679 common rows and comparing them with the labels from the model refit on just those rows gives an adjusted Rand index of 0.887, and after Hungarian matching 94.9% of the common rows fall in the same matched component. The matched component profiles line up closely as well: height, shot selection, playmaking, rebounding, and blocks differ by at most 0.8 units between the two models in every component (0.8 cm for one component's height; everything else differs by 0.3 or less). Removing the lowest-participation rows therefore does not change which roles the model finds.

Checking whether a component is really a recording-period effect¶

The coordinate-system comparison earlier found that the undocumented zone letters, not the coordinates themselves, differ between E2007-E2008 and the rest of the data. The clustering features use only the raw coordinate summaries, which we found compatible across periods, but we checked directly whether any of the five components is disproportionately made up of E2007-E2008 observations, since that would point to a methodological artifact rather than a playing-style role.

None of the five components is disproportionately made up of early-period rows. The overall eligible sample is 10.8% E2007-E2008, and the per-component share ranges from 8.4% (component 2) to 14.8% (component 4) -- a narrow band around the overall share, not the near-exclusive concentration we saw for the exact zero-attempt and zero-block point masses earlier. The recording-period difference in the zone letters does not drive the discovered components, so we did not run a further sensitivity comparison here.

The five-component GMM holds up under all three checks: it does not depend on the random initialization, it reappears with closely matching profiles under a stricter participation rule, and no component is an artifact of the recording-period difference between the earliest two seasons and the rest. We therefore treat it as a stable result and move on to interpreting what each component represents.

Interpreting the five components¶

With the five-component GMM shown to be a stable result, we turned to what each component actually represents: its feature profile, the players it contains, and whether that profile and those players support a basketball role.

Each component has a clear set of standardized means that set it apart from the others, so we went through them one at a time, citing both the standardized mean and the raw-unit mean from the table above.

Component 0 stands out for assists per 40 (z = +0.88, 4.84 raw) and turnovers per 40 (z = +0.54, 2.97), together with below-average height (z = -0.79, 192.8 cm), offensive rebounds (z = -0.72, 0.85), and blocks (z = -0.56, 0.16). This is the profile of a player who creates and carries the ball more than the other components, and plays away from the basket on defense and the offensive glass. We call it playmaking guards.

Component 1 is the most extreme profile in the whole solution: its shot-distance spread (z = -1.90, 127.7 raw units) and lateral spread (z = -1.73, 140.4) are both far below every other component, three-point attempts per 40 are essentially zero (z = -1.50, 0.12), and height (z = +1.13, 209.3 cm), offensive rebounds (z = +1.50, 3.78), and blocks (z = +1.29, 1.38) are all far above average. These are players whose shots come from one small area near the basket and almost nowhere else. We call it low-post centers.

Component 2 has no standardized mean larger than 0.66 in absolute value -- clearly the flattest of the five. Its largest signals are below-average turnovers (z = -0.55, 1.88) and fouls received (z = -0.47, 3.16), with mildly above-average shot-distance and lateral spread (z = +0.66 and +0.52). Height (202.0 cm) and every shot-selection feature sit close to the sample average. This looks like a genuinely lower-usage role rather than a role defined by one strong signal, so we kept the name simple: low-usage forwards.

Component 3 is the mirror image of component 1 in shot location: the longest median shot distance of the five (z = +1.23, 696.2 raw units), the most three-point attempts per 40 (z = +1.01, 7.18), the fewest two-point attempts (z = -0.93, 4.47), and the widest lateral spread of shots (z = +0.88, 406.4). Offensive rebounding is low (z = -0.72, 0.85), consistent with a player who plays away from the basket. We call it perimeter shooters.

Component 4 combines above-average height (z = +0.73, 205.8 cm), defensive and offensive rebounding (z = +0.75 and +0.72), blocks (z = +0.52, 0.87), and two-point attempts per 40 (z = +0.72, 9.67 -- the second-highest of any component) with a median shot distance well short of average (z = -0.93, 226.8) but nowhere near as extreme as component 1's 147.6, and a non-trivial three-point rate (2.66 per 40 against component 1's 0.12). These are big, productive interior players who still shoot from more than one spot on the floor. We call it mobile stretch bigs.

To check these profiles against real players rather than only summary statistics, we listed three representative player-season-team observations per component: those closest to the mean of their own component. We measured closeness with the Mahalanobis distance under that component's fitted covariance matrix, in the same standardized feature space used for clustering, so a feature that varies widely within a role counts less than one the role holds tightly, and correlated features are not counted twice. Each player appears at most once per component, and exact ties are broken by player_id, season, and team.

In [80]:
def mahalanobis_to_own_component(X, labels, gmm):
    distances = pd.Series(np.nan, index=X.index)
    for component in range(gmm.n_components):
        in_component = (labels == component).to_numpy()
        diff = X.to_numpy()[in_component] - gmm.means_[component]
        whitened = diff @ gmm.precisions_cholesky_[component]
        distances.iloc[np.flatnonzero(in_component)] = np.sqrt((whitened ** 2).sum(axis=1))
    return distances


representatives = (
    modeling_metadata.assign(
        component=gmm_labels,
        distance=mahalanobis_to_own_component(X_scaled, gmm_labels, gmm_selected))
    .sort_values(["component", "distance", "player_id", "season_code", "team_id"],
                 kind="mergesort")
    .drop_duplicates(subset=["component", "player_id"], keep="first")
    .groupby("component").head(3)
)
representatives["example"] = (representatives["player"] + " (" + representatives["season_code"]
                              + ", " + representatives["team_id"] + ")")
representatives["rank"] = representatives.groupby("component").cumcount() + 1

representative_table = (representatives.pivot(index="component", columns="rank", values="example")
                        .rename(index=ROLE_NAMES)
                        .rename_axis(index="role", columns="example"))
representative_table

In every component, the observations closest to the mean belong to players whose known playing style matches the role's statistical profile: lead ball handlers among the playmaking guards, interior centers among the low-post centers, perimeter-oriented guards and wings among the perimeter shooters, and frontcourt players who also shoot from farther out among the mobile stretch bigs. The low-usage forwards are forwards rather than primary ball handlers or post players, which supports reading component 2 as a genuine, if broad, role rather than a statistical leftover. Because these are typical rather than extreme members, they show what an ordinary observation of each role looks like.

A player who changes role¶

Because player-season-team is the unit of observation, a player who appears in several eligible seasons can fall into different components over their career. We looked for a case where that change tells a coherent story rather than reflecting noise between two similar components, and found one in Alberto Abalde.

abalde["role_name"] = abalde["component"].map(ROLE_NAMES)
abalde["posterior"] = max_posterior.loc[abalde.index]
abalde.sort_values("season_code")[["season_code", "team_id", "component", "role_name",

In his first eligible season (E2017, at Joventut) Abalde is a playmaking guard (component 0, posterior 0.83); from E2020 onward, after moving to Real Madrid, he is a perimeter shooter (component 3) in five of his six seasons there, with one season (E2021) as a low-usage forward (component 2). The shift is consistent with a change in role from a young player given the ball more at a smaller club to a catch-and-shoot wing on a deeper roster. The clustering tracks this change using only the season's statistics, without being told anything about Abalde's career or his team.

None of the five components looked incoherent enough to revise the model over: each has a distinct standardized profile (even component 2, whose profile is comparatively flat), real players whose statistics and -- where we recognized them -- known games match the role, and in Abalde's case, a sensible within-career trajectory from one role to another.

Comparing the roles with traditional positions¶

Position labels were never used as a clustering input -- we used them only now, to see whether the five discovered roles reveal distinctions that the traditional position labels do not. position_reconciled (the five-category label built from 365scores and Wikipedia) is the main comparison, and the three-category EuroLeague position is a coarser, supplementary check, the same roles for the two labels decided when we built the feature table.

Reading down each position's column shows how far a single traditional position can split into different roles. Center is the most concentrated position: 69% of Centers are low-post centers and 24% are mobile stretch bigs, two roles with clearly different profiles -- almost no three-point shooting for low-post centers, against a real three-point rate for mobile stretch bigs. Point Guard is similarly concentrated but into a different two-role split: 54% playmaking guards and 40% perimeter shooters. Shooting Guard splits almost the same way (44% perimeter shooters, 36% playmaking guards), but with the two roles' shares reversed, so the official point guard/shooting guard distinction does not line up cleanly with the ball-handling-versus-shooting distinction the roles capture -- many nominal point guards are mainly shooters and many nominal shooting guards are mainly ball-handlers. Small Forward and Power Forward are the least concentrated: Small Forward splits across low-usage forwards (42%), perimeter shooters (30%), and playmaking guards (16%), and Power Forward splits across low-usage forwards (37%), mobile stretch bigs (31%), and low-post centers (18%).

The same pattern appears from the role side. Low-post centers and playmaking guards each draw almost entirely from one or two positions that are already similar to each other (74% Center + 23% Power Forward; 52% Point Guard + 30% Shooting Guard), so these two roles mostly refine positions that were already close. Low-usage forwards and mobile stretch bigs instead each combine two positions that the label keeps separate: low-usage forwards are 38% Small Forward and 37% Power Forward, and mobile stretch bigs are 50% Power Forward and 31% Center, spanning the forward-center line that position_reconciled treats as a hard boundary.

Adjusted Rand index, roles vs position_reconciled (5-category, primary): 0.210
Adjusted Rand index, roles vs position (3-category, supplementary): 0.288

Both adjusted Rand indices are low -- 0.210 against the five-category position_reconciled and 0.288 against the coarser three-category position -- far below the 0.4-0.5 agreement between our own K-Means and GMM solutions. The index is likely a little higher for the coarser label because collapsing Point Guard/Shooting Guard and Small Forward/Power Forward into Guard/Forward removes some of the within-position splits our roles create, rather than because it captures more of the role structure.

Given the splits and merges above, we treat the discovered roles as adding real information beyond the position labels, not as a finer-grained restatement of them, and not because there are more roles than positions.

Discussion¶

The eligible player-season-team rows separate into five roles: playmaking guards, low-post centers, low-usage forwards, perimeter shooters, and mobile stretch bigs, each with its own standardized profile and representative players. We reached this result with a full-covariance Gaussian mixture on the 17 standardized features, with K-Means as a simpler baseline. A small covariance regularization was needed to keep the likelihood from rewarding components collapsed onto the exact zero-attempt and zero-block point masses; under it, BIC selected five components, with six as a close alternative.

The five-component solution reproduced closely across ten random initializations, reappeared with matching profiles on the stricter participation sample, and showed no component tied to the earliest recorded seasons. Within these checks, we treat it as a stable result rather than an artifact of one fit, while it remains conditional on the feature set and the regularization.

The roles are also not simply a repackaging of the traditional positions: the adjusted Rand index is low against both position_reconciled (0.210) and position (0.288), well below the 0.4-0.5 agreement between our own K-Means and GMM solutions. The clearest evidence is the split of Centers into low-post centers and mobile stretch bigs and the two roles that combine positions the labels keep separate, not the number of roles. Within the limitations below, this answers our research question: unsupervised learning on player-season-team performance data, without any position input, finds interpretable roles that carry information beyond the traditional positions.

Limitations¶

The robustness checks and the position comparison are backed by direct evidence above. The points below are choices and assumptions we did not test as thoroughly.

  • Participation threshold. The 5-games/100-minutes rule decides which rows enter the model. A stricter rule reproduced the same roles, but we did not test a looser one.
  • Feature representation. The 17 features, the shrinkage of the shooting percentages, and the choice among correlated candidates are defensible but not the only possible choices; a different feature set could emphasize other aspects of play.
  • Regularization. Five components were selected under both reg_covar = 0.01 and 0.1, but the regularization is still a modeling assumption, and k = 6 was close behind in BIC.
  • Shot data. Shot-type detail and the zone letters are not recorded consistently across seasons, so we use only the coordinate summaries, whose units are undocumented. Standardization puts them on a common numeric scale, but it does not by itself show that coordinates were recorded consistently across seasons, and we cannot state distances in meters.
  • Change over time. No component is tied to the two earliest seasons, but we did not test for a more gradual drift in playing style over the 19 seasons.
  • Overlapping roles. The PCA projection showed a continuum rather than separated groups, and 3.5% of rows have a largest membership probability below 0.6, so some rows sit between roles rather than inside one; the Gaussian components impose elliptical groups on that continuum.
  • Repeated players. A player active for many eligible seasons contributes many rows, so role sizes count player-seasons, not distinct players.
  • Missing position labels. 2.2% (position_reconciled) and 2.9% (position) of eligible rows have no label and are left out of the comparison. We expect this small share to have little effect, but we did not test it.
